source: Asset: branding/National Show 2027/Logo/NOS-2027-logo-full-colour-vertical.png, confirmed with Brad per team lead's dispatch (2026-09-11). Native pixel dimensions read directly from the PNG IHDR chunk (not assumed): 3272x2876px, aspect ratio (w/h) = 1.13769 -- i.e. very slightly wider than tall, despite the 'vertical' name (which distinguishes this lockup from a horizontal wordmark-beside-flower variant, not a literal portrait aspect ratio). Visually inspected (2026-09-11): a botanical illustration of a single orchid bloom above two lines of serif/mono text -- 'NATIONAL ORCHID SHOW' (tracked-caps serif, royal-purple ink) and, below a thin rule, 'WESTERN CAPE · 2027' (tracked-caps mono/sans, olive ink). No SAOC wordmark, no edition number ('19th'), no venue name, and no specific dates appear anywhere on the artwork.

Both are folded into one visual unit today (a small mono caption directly above a serif link) and the logo image itself already carries the equivalent identity content ('National Orchid Show', plus 'Western Cape · 2027') -- keeping the eyebrow text as a separate sibling above the image would duplicate what the artwork already says and contradicts Brad's plain reading of 'replace the heading... with the logo', not 'add the logo above the heading'.
reading.metaLineRuling: KEEP leadMeta (venue name + formatted date range, rendered today via formatShowDateRange from the nationalShow Sanity singleton -- see MegaMenu.tsx's leadMeta computation) directly below the logo image, unchanged in its own rendering logic. Brad's instruction named only 'the heading' -- the logo does NOT carry the specific venue name (e.g. 'The Hangar, Stellenbosch Flying Club') or exact show dates, only the province and year, so dropping leadMeta would be a real information regression on the one piece of practical information ('where and when') a menu visitor is most likely to want. Do not remove it; do not fold it into alt text as a substitute for on-page text -- alt text is not a substitute for visible content per WCAG, and screen-reader users need leadMeta rendered exactly as sighted users see it.
reading.theShowGroupRuling: UNCHANGED. Brad's instruction addressed only the heading text, not the 'The Show' links list beneath it (Tickets / Show Sponsors / etc. leaves) -- no reading of his instruction extends to removing navigational leaves.

containerBudget.computation: Grid track ratios (F7, unchanged): [1.05fr, 1fr, 1fr, 1fr, .9fr], sum 5. Outer wrapper: mx-auto max-w-[1280px] px-8 (32px each side) -> inner content width at >=1280px viewport = 1280 - 64 = 1216px. Lead track width = 1216 * (1.05/5) = 255.4px. Lead block's own padding-right (pr-6, 24px, unchanged from F7) leaves 231.4px of actual content width.
containerBudget.note: 200px image width (above) fits inside the 231px budget with an 11px margin against layout noise (sub-pixel `fr` rounding, borders) -- verified by real measurement in the e2e golden below, not assumed from this arithmetic alone. The image must NOT be styled at 100% of the track width (231px) with zero margin -- that leaves no breathing room and risks a 1-2px overflow into the Visit column's border-left at narrower-than-1440px real-world viewports.

backgroundRuling.source: NOS Design session, R21, 2026-09-17, verbatim: "Two conditions on the lockup lead block: ... No plate behind it. The supplied files ship transparent with clearspace built in, and the production sheet's tinted panel is preview only. Pick a supplied colourway that works on your panel's ground -- never re-tint, never re-typeset, and don't add a tinted rectangle to make a mismatched colourway sit. If none of the eight colourways works on that ground, tell me; that is a design question and it is mine."
backgroundRuling.rule: No element between the and the mega-menu panel (role="menu", bg-parchment) may carry an added background-color. The PNG ships transparent -- the only permissible ground behind the artwork is the panel's own bg-parchment showing through, never a plate/rectangle/tint introduced by the lead block or any of its wrapping elements. This is independent of which of the eight supplied colourways is used -- it prohibits an added plate regardless of colourway choice.

priorSelfConfirmedNote.reasoning: The panel ground is --color-parchment (#f4f3ec, app/globals.css:13/116), a light warm off-white. The full-colour artwork's ink (source above: royal-purple #211A57 for 'NATIONAL ORCHID SHOW', olive for 'WESTERN CAPE · 2027') is dark-on-light -- both inks are near-black-value hues with high contrast against #f4f3ec, the same relationship the reversed-white/reversed-gold colourways exist to avoid on a DARK ground. If the rendered artwork visually clashes once placed (a property only a rendered screenshot can show), that is still NOS Design's call per their own reservation clause, not a reason to swap colourways unilaterally.

minRenderedWidthRuling.status: SUPERSEDED 2026-09-19 -- the ~120px figure below is RETRACTED by NOS Design. Kept verbatim for provenance; do not re-derive or re-cite the 120px number as authoritative. See `correctedTable` for the current figures and `retractionSource` for why.
minRenderedWidthRuling.source: NOS Design session, verbatim, 2026-09-17 (SUPERSEDED, see status above): "One real constraint that came out of looking -- and it is new, so take it as a ruling. The palest petal tips come closest to the ground of anything in the file, so the flower's outer silhouette is the first thing to go. Set a minimum rendered size for `full-colour` on any light ground, and do not scale the vertical lockup below roughly 120px wide there. Below that the pale laterals stop resolving as petals and the mark starts reading as a purple blob with type under it. On dark grounds this does not arise -- that is what the reversed colourways are for. If your lead block is smaller than that, tell me and I will pick a different colourway rather than have you shrink this one."
minRenderedWidthRuling.rule: SUPERSEDED -- see `correctedTable`. Original text (kept for provenance only, do not apply): full-colour, on any light ground (bg-parchment included), must never render narrower than ~120px wide. Below that threshold the pale petal tips (the artwork's lowest-contrast region against a light ground) stop resolving and the mark degrades to an unreadable blob. This does not apply on dark grounds -- the reversed colourways exist for that case and carry no such floor per NOS Design.
minRenderedWidthRuling.retractionSource: NOS Design, 2026-09-19, verbatim: the ~120px figure was retracted -- "the figure was a measurement artifact from an upscaled evidence plate," i.e. it was derived from a plate that had itself already been scaled up, not from the real artwork at real size, so the number it produced was never a genuine legibility threshold. The 'petal legibility' rationale attached to the original 120px figure is the artifact's own rationale, not a real finding, and must not be cited as if it were.

slotTypeRuling.status: CORRECTED 2026-09-19 -- the mega-menu lead block is NOT a hero slot. This golden's own earlier `currentMargin` note classified it into the corrected table's 160-220px 'heroes' band; that classification is wrong and is replaced by this ruling.
slotTypeRuling.reasoning: A hero is page-level and appears once per page; the mega-menu lead block is transient chrome -- open on hover/focus, sharing the sheet with four other nav-group tracks, dismissed on blur/close. By slot type it is 'general use', the corrected table's 120px row, not 'heroes'.
slotTypeRuling.sourceForKeepingRenderAt200: NOS Design, verbatim, 2026-09-19: keep the render at 200px anyway. The corrected table's bands are FLOORS, not ceilings -- 120px is where 'general use' is clean, not a ceiling above which rendering is wrong. The lead block is the one moment the show gets a visual statement inside SAOC's chrome, so erring large (200px, comfortably inside the 'heroes' band's pixel range even though this is not a hero slot) is the correct choice by NOS Design's own direction, not a misclassification propagating forward.
slotTypeRuling.conclusion: render.widthPx stays 200 -- same number as before this correction. What changes is ONLY the stated reason: it is not 200px because the lead block IS a hero, it is 200px because NOS Design deliberately chose to place a general-use slot above its own floor. Do not let this correction be misread as a mandate to shrink the render to 120px -- NOS Design's own instruction (quoted above) is the opposite: keep 200px.

minRenderedWidthRuling.gateDecision: STILL not adding a minimum-rendered-width contract assertion, for the same reason as before the retraction: render.widthPx (200) and containerBudget.maxWidthPx (220) are fixed numeric literals, not props/CSS driven by viewport or config, and 200px falls inside the corrected table's top 'heroes' band regardless of which of the table's rows is treated as the operative minimum. Revisit if widthPx is ever made responsive (e.g. driven by track fr-ratio at runtime rather than a literal) -- at that point add a minimum-width assertion alongside A2's existing max-width check, sized against the corrected table above, never against the retracted 120px figure.

servingResolutionRuling.enforcementBanner: SUPERSEDED 2026-09-21 -- do NOT trust this banner's own conclusion. This banner originally said 'A12 IS LIVE AND ENFORCED TODAY... the underlying rule R22... is NOT retracted, remains true... Do not read the retraction language below as license to remove A12.' That was correct on 2026-09-19 when written; it is no longer true. See `withdrawalRecord` immediately below `id` for the full, later, WHOLE-RULE withdrawal -- R22 itself (not just its NOS-pages causal application, which is the narrower `premiseRetraction` this banner was originally warning readers not to over-read) is now withdrawn in full by NOS Design, with Brad's own asset-handling instruction independently settling the same question. A12 is NOT dead, but it is re-grounded on entirely different reasoning that has nothing to do with R22 -- see contract-f8.yaml's A12 for what it checks now. Kept verbatim below, unedited, so a reader can see exactly what this banner claimed and when it stopped being true -- this is the second time a banner/status field in this object has needed a correction layered on top of it (see `premiseRetraction` below for the first), which is itself worth noticing before trusting a third.

withdrawalRecord.status: R22 WITHDRAWN IN FULL, 2026-09-21. This is a stronger action than `premiseRetraction` below (2026-09-19), which only narrowed R22's claim about WHY the NOS pages looked bad while leaving the underlying rule (2x source floor, derive from master) standing and enforced via A12. This withdrawal kills the underlying rule itself -- the 400px floor, the 'generate every derivative from the master' prescription, and the contract assertion policing export widths are all dead, not narrowed.
withdrawalRecord.who: NOS Design, via their commit 0a79280, relayed by the team lead together with Brad's own direct instruction as the independent, governing authority.
withdrawalRecord.reasoning: NOS Design's own reasoning: the vertical master is 3272px and the horizontal master is 4108px, against a 200px CSS render -- roughly 16x oversampled before any Retina 2x multiplier is even applied. The serving-resolution problem R22 described only ever existed under the assumption that sized derivatives would be cut from the masters to some target width; used as supplied (the full, un-cut master file placed directly), that assumption never arises, so there is nothing for a density floor to protect against.
withdrawalRecord.bradsInstruction: Quoted directly, and treated as the independent, second, sufficient reason this floor is dead even without NOS Design's own withdrawal: "Keep the fucking branding assets as I supplied them. Don't convert edit or change anything. You place it on the page and that's it." A workflow with no processing step has no derivative-generation step for a 2x-density floor to police in the first place.
withdrawalRecord.secondRetractionNote: R22 has now been retracted twice in this golden, in two different ways -- worth flagging so a third citation of it is checked, not assumed. First (2026-09-19, `premiseRetraction` below): NARROWED -- only the specific causal claim about the NOS pages' own pixelation was withdrawn; the general rule and its application to F8a stood, and A12 kept enforcing it. Second (2026-09-21, this record): WITHDRAWN IN FULL -- the general rule itself is now dead, for this feature and everywhere else, on NOS Design's own authority plus Brad's independent asset policy. A ruling that has been narrowed once and killed once should not be cited a third time without checking it is still live -- it is not, as of this record.
withdrawalRecord.whatA12BecomesInstead: contract-f8.yaml's A12 is RE-GROUNDED, not deleted -- see that assertion's full reasoning. Summary: the width-floor check (the only one of the checker's six checks that depended on R22) is removed entirely. The other five structural-integrity checks (PNG signature, IHDR-is-first-chunk, IHDR length == 13, IEND terminator present, at least one IDAT chunk present) and the exact-basename check (`caseSensitivityRuling` below) survive, re-justified on their own merits -- they catch a bad hand-copy of the master, which is exactly the operation Brad's 'place it, don't process it' policy still requires a human to get right, independent of R22 ever having existed.

servingResolutionRuling.source: NOS Design, verbatim, 2026-09-19: "The real cause of the bad rendering on the NOS pages is not size, it is serving resolution. A Retina display wants two device pixels per CSS pixel, so a lockup occupying 200 CSS px needs a source at least 400px wide. The masters are ample (vertical 3272px, horizontal 4108px), so pixelation means a small or already-downscaled export is being served, or CSS is stretching a raster past 100% of its natural width. So when you place the lockup: generate the derivative from the master, never from another derivative, and never let it render wider than its natural pixel width."
servingResolutionRuling.distinctionFromMinRenderedWidthRuling: This is a DIFFERENT risk from the (now-superseded) minRenderedWidthRuling above. That ruling was about the rendered CSS width being too small for the eye to resolve petal detail at any source resolution. R22 is about the SOURCE FILE's own pixel resolution being too small (or too-downscaled) relative to a fixed rendered CSS width -- a source-provenance defect, not a layout-sizing one. A file can pass every layout/CSS-width check in this golden (A1-A3, A11) and still fail R22 if it is, say, a 200px-wide export instead of a derivative of the 3272x2876px master documented in `asset` above.
servingResolutionRuling.failureMode: Human, not code: Brad hand-copies the runtime asset (see `asset.runtimeTargetPath`) from the branding/ master into public/images/. If he exports/copies a downscaled version instead of a true derivative of the 3272px master, the lead block renders soft on every Retina screen -- and prior to this ruling, NO assertion in this contract could catch it, because A1-A3 and A11 all read the rendered DOM, and a 200px-wide source and a 3272px-wide source render at the IDENTICAL 200 CSS px. The DOM is indistinguishable. This is this project's own audited 'assertion satisfiable without the property it claims to prove' defect class (see contract-f8.yaml A9's framing of the same class for a different check).
servingResolutionRuling.verifiedFacts: Master dimensions (3272x2876px) are already read directly from the PNG IHDR chunk and documented in `asset` above -- not re-derived here. The IHDR-read technique (bytes 16-19 = width, 20-23 = height, big-endian uint32, after the 8-byte PNG signature + 4-byte length + 4-byte 'IHDR' tag) is the same technique the new checker script uses.
servingResolutionRuling.uncitedGap: MOOT as of the 2026-09-21 withdrawal (kept for provenance, not live): next/image's behaviour when the SOURCE file itself is narrower than a requested 2x/400px srcset candidate is NOT confirmed by any doc fetched during research (see .agent/memory/scratch/research-menu-system-layout4-f8-retina.md finding 3) -- whether the optimizer caps the derivative at the source's native width (and the browser upscales/stretches it) or something else. This golden does not assert or rely on that mechanism; the new assertion below checks the SOURCE FILE directly, independent of what next/image does with it, so the gap does not weaken it. Moot now because there is no 400px comparison left in A12 to weaken -- the gap was only ever relevant to a width-floor check that no longer exists.

premiseRetraction.status: R22's NOS-pages causal claim is RETRACTED as of 2026-09-19. The serving-resolution FINDING itself (2x device-pixel density, generate derivatives from the master, never from another derivative) is NOT retracted and remains the live basis for A12 below -- do not read this note as walking back A12.
premiseRetraction.source: NOS Design, verbatim, 2026-09-19: Brad's original pixelation complaint was made while looking at NOS Design's own review artifact -- their evidence plate, not the live NOS Site. They corrected that plate, then generalised the defect into a causal claim about the NOS pages themselves ("the real cause of the bad rendering on the NOS pages is not size, it is serving resolution") -- a claim about pages the same artifact had already stated they could not see. "Same error class, twice": inferring a false 120px CSS floor from a blurry plate, then a false diagnosis of another session's live pages from that same blurry plate.
premiseRetraction.contradictingEvidence: The NOS Site audit found NO raster NOS logo exists on those pages at all -- vector emblem only (see R23 below, EmblemBadge.tsx composes an SVG emblem, not a raster export). A raster serving-resolution defect cannot reproduce against a page that never serves a raster logo, so the specific NOS-pages diagnosis does not hold.
premiseRetraction.whatStandsVsWhatIsWithdrawn: STANDS: the general rule (a lockup rendered at N CSS px on a Retina display needs a source >= 2N px wide, sourced from the master, not a derivative-of-a-derivative) and its application to F8a's own logo placement -- F8a genuinely places a raster PNG at 200 CSS px, so the 400px floor and A12 are real, warranted checks for THIS feature regardless of what caused the NOS pages issue. WITHDRAWN: the specific claim that this explains the NOS Site's pixelation, and any inference that the NOS pages carry a too-small raster export needing the same fix -- they do not carry a raster export to begin with.
premiseRetraction.recordKeepingNote: Same treatment as the 120px retraction below: do not delete the ruling or A12. The verbatim R22 quote in `source` above is retained for provenance with its NOS-pages sentence intact -- a future reader must see that the sentence was part of the original ruling and was later narrowed, not that the whole ruling evaporated. A12 remains enforced wherever this project places a raster identity asset.

assertionDecision.status: HISTORICAL -- describes the now-withdrawn width-floor decision. Kept verbatim for provenance; superseded by `withdrawalRecord.whatA12BecomesInstead` above and by contract-f8.yaml's re-grounded A12, which the checker now implements with the width floor removed and the other five integrity checks plus the exact-basename check re-justified independently of R22.
assertionDecision.verdict: ADDED -- contract-f8.yaml A12, backed by a new checker: contracts/checks/menu-system-layout4-f8/check-logo-source-resolution.mjs.
assertionDecision.reasoning: This is exactly the defect class this project has already burned time on (see A9's framing, and project memory feedback_contract_scoring_principles): a real, human-triggerable failure mode with zero existing coverage, and the fix is a direct, cheap, non-invented check (read the IHDR width of the file that already gets placed at a known path, compare against 2x of the already-specified 200px render width = 400px minimum). Not adding it would leave the exact gap R22 was raised to close.
assertionDecision.sequencing: The checker is written to vacuous-pass (exit 0, informational message) when the runtime asset does not exist yet -- it does NOT duplicate A10's job of gating on absence, and does not red the gate ahead of Brad placing the file. It only fails when a file IS present and its IHDR width is below the 400px minimum. This means, unlike A10 (required: false, expected-fail-until-placed), A12 can safely be `required: true` from the start: it is vacuously green today, stays green if a correctly-sized file lands, and only turns red on the actual defect (a present-but-undersized/re-exported file) -- a check that passes on absence AND passes on a bad file would be worthless, per the team lead's brief; this one passes on absence but genuinely fails on a bad file.
assertionDecision.minWidthChosen: 400px -- exactly R22's own worked example (200 CSS px rendered width x 2 device px per CSS px = 400px), matching this golden's render.widthPx (200) precisely rather than a rounded or invented figure.

derivationRule.status: HISTORICAL -- the width floor this derivation supported no longer exists. Kept verbatim for provenance only; do not use `sourceFloorPx = 2 x renderedWidthPx` to justify re-adding a width check on this golden's authority. See `withdrawalRecord` above.
derivationRule.statement: NOS Design, verbatim, 2026-09-19: "the source floor follows the rendered size you actually chose, never the name of the slot." Record as a DERIVATION, not a pair of fixed numbers: sourceFloorPx = 2 x renderedWidthPx (Retina 2x density). At today's chosen render.widthPx (200), the floor is 400px -- that is a consequence of the 200px choice, not an independent fact. If render.widthPx is ever changed (e.g. the lead block drops to the 120px 'general use' figure per `slotTypeRuling` below), the floor changes with it to 240px; it does not stay pinned at 400px.

literalCouplingRisk.status: MOOT -- the coupling this risk describes (checker's 400 vs. golden's 200) no longer exists once the width floor is removed from A12's command line. Kept for provenance; no follow-up action remains.
literalCouplingRisk.finding: contract-f8.yaml A12's command line passes 400 and 200 as two independent literal arguments (`check-logo-source-resolution.mjs <path> 400 200`) -- there is no code-level expression tying the 400 to '2 x 200'. If a future change edits render.widthPx (this golden) or the rendered CSS width in MegaMenu.tsx without also editing A12's command-line literal, A12 silently keeps checking the OLD floor against the NEW render width -- it would still exit 0/1 correctly relative to its own stale 400px argument, but that argument would no longer be 2x of what actually renders, and the assertion would be checking the wrong property without any error to signal it.
literalCouplingRisk.ruling: Acceptable as-is for now, not urgent: render.widthPx (200) is presently a fixed numeric literal in this golden and in MegaMenu.tsx's implementation, not viewport- or config-driven -- the two literals (checker's 400 and golden's 200) only drift if a human edits one and forgets the other, which is the same class of risk as any two independently-maintained constants. NOT acceptable to leave unaddressed indefinitely: flagging as a follow-up, not fixing here (I do not touch the checker -- @dev owns check-logo-source-resolution.mjs and is concurrently editing it). Recommended follow-up for whoever next touches A12 or render.widthPx: either (a) derive the 400 from a shared constant/prop rather than a second literal, or (b) add a same-file comment on both the golden's render.widthPx and A12's command line cross-referencing each other so an editor changing one is prompted to check the other. Do not silently duplicate this fix into the checker script myself -- out of scope for this pass and inside @dev's concurrently-edited file.
literalCouplingRisk.qaConcurrence: @qa independently reviewed this same coupling and reached the identical ruling: real risk, but no automatic drift is possible today because both the checker's 400 and this golden's render.widthPx (200) are static literals -- drift requires a human to edit one and forget the other, and `derivationRule` above already documents the 2x relationship for that human to consult. @qa's PASS verdict on A12/F8 treats this as a recorded follow-up, not a blocking defect. Keep it a follow-up, not a fix, unless render.widthPx becomes viewport- or config-driven (see `gateDecision` above for the equivalent condition already stated for the minimum-width case).

caseSensitivityRuling.status: NEW ENFORCED PROPERTY of A12, recorded 2026-09-19 -- this is not a note about existing behaviour, it is a defect A12 now actively closes. CONFIRMED STILL LIVE 2026-09-21: unaffected by R22's full withdrawal above -- this check never depended on R22 or on any width value, only on exact-basename matching via a real directory listing, so it survives A12's re-grounding unchanged and stays part of the same checker/assertion.
caseSensitivityRuling.finding: @qa found, and the team lead independently reproduced directly on this machine, that macOS/APFS is case-INSENSITIVE but case-PRESERVING for path lookups by default: with a file named `NOS-TEST-Logo.png` present in a directory, BOTH `test -f .../nos-test-logo.png` (shell) and Node's `fs.existsSync('.../nos-test-logo.png')` return true against the differently-cased real file -- the filesystem silently resolves the lowercase query to the title-cased file on disk. Only an explicit directory listing exposes the true on-disk name: `fs.readdirSync(dir).includes('nos-test-logo.png')` correctly returns false, because it compares the exact string against the real filenames rather than asking the filesystem to resolve a path.
caseSensitivityRuling.consequence: Without a fix, a mis-cased hand-copy of the runtime asset (e.g. Brad copies `NOS-2027-Logo-Full-Colour-Vertical.png` instead of exactly `nos-2027-logo-full-colour-vertical.png` into public/images/) produces ACTIVE FALSE CONFIDENCE, not a vacuous pass: A10 (`test -f`, case-blind by construction -- see below) reports the asset present, and A12 reads the IHDR width off the real file and reports a correct 3272px width, so A12 PASSES. The whole contract goes green. But Firebase App Hosting runs on Linux, which is case-SENSITIVE -- the exact lowercase path this project's code requests (`asset.runtimeTargetPath` above) does not exist there, and the asset 404s in production while every local/contract check said it was fine. The trigger scenario is ordinary, not exotic: design exports are frequently delivered title-cased, and the workflow is Brad hand-copying the file (see `asset.note` above) rather than a scripted, case-normalising copy.
caseSensitivityRuling.closingFix: @dev is adding an exact-basename check to check-logo-source-resolution.mjs (A12), with three states -- recorded here so the property survives even though @dev owns the file and this record-keeping pass does not touch it: (1) no case-variant of the expected filename present in the directory -- unchanged vacuous PASS, same as today; (2) a case-variant is present (i.e. a lowercase-insensitive match exists via directory listing) but it is NOT an exact match to the expected lowercase basename -- FAIL, this is the defect case; (3) an exact basename match exists -- proceed to all existing IHDR-width checks as before. The mechanism is the `readdirSync`-vs-`existsSync` distinction found above: exact matching must walk the real directory listing, never trust a resolved existsSync/test -f result as proof of the real on-disk name.
caseSensitivityRuling.whyA10DoesNotCatchThis: A10 (`test -f`, gating on the runtime asset's mere presence) is explicitly case-blind by construction -- it is a shell existence check, subject to the exact same APFS case-folding behaviour documented in `finding` above, so a mis-cased file makes A10 report present exactly as readily as a correctly-cased one. A10 was never designed to catch this and should not be modified to try -- A12's exact-basename check is the correct, and only, place in this contract that closes the hole, which is a second, independent reason (beyond `enforcementBanner` above) that A12 must stay enforced and must not be simplified back to a bare `existsSync` check by a future editor who does not know this history.

acceptedLimitations.status: Deliberate scope decisions under a stated threat model, recorded so a future reader does not rediscover them as if they were newly-found oversights. Threat model throughout: an HONEST hand-copy of a real design export by Brad, per the established workflow (see `asset.note` above) -- there is no adversary uploading a crafted file. Full PNG validation would require a real decoder (zlib inflation, bit-depth/colour-type/interlace handling, IDAT-vs-IHDR cross-checks); A12 is deliberately fast and dependency-free, reading only the IHDR header bytes, and these are the known, accepted gaps that leaves open.

declaredWidthForgery.status: CLOSED BY REMOVAL, 2026-09-21 -- not merely accepted anymore. This entire finding was about A12 trusting a WIDTH claim it could not verify; once the width floor is removed (R22 withdrawal, see `withdrawalRecord` above), A12 makes no width claim at all, so there is nothing left for a forged width to deceive. This is a genuine, incidental closure of the exact attack surface @qa demonstrated, not a re-acceptance of the same risk under a new name -- record it as closed, not as still-accepted.
declaredWidthForgery.finding: @qa built genuinely valid, zlib-deflated PNGs where the IHDR width field bytes were hand-patched to claim 500px width while the IDAT chunk actually carried real, correctly-compressed pixel data for a 40x40 image (and, separately, another fixture for a 1x1 image). A12 reads only the IHDR width bytes and reports these fixtures as passing the 400px floor. `sips` (macOS's real decoder) fails to decode them, or decodes them to their true smaller dimensions -- the declared width and the actual image content disagree, and A12 has no way to detect that disagreement because it never reads or inflates the IDAT chunk. A separate fixture with a spec-illegal bit-depth byte (bytes 24-28 of the PNG, which A12 never reads: bit depth, colour type, compression method, filter method, interlace method) also passes A12 while failing to decode in a real decoder.
declaredWidthForgery.rootCause: A12 trusts the raw IHDR width field with zero correlation to decoded IDAT content, and never validates bytes 24-28 (bit depth / colour type / compression / filter / interlace) at all -- it is a header-read, not a decode.
declaredWidthForgery.rulingHistorical: Kept for provenance only, no longer the live ruling (see `status` above): originally 'Accepted, not fixed' under the stated threat model (honest hand-copy, no adversary constructing a hostile PNG) -- nobody hand-copying a design export from branding/ produces a file with a forged IHDR width and mismatched IDAT content, and closing it fully would have required a real PNG decoder, a materially larger dependency than this check's design goal warranted. Superseded because the premise (A12 checks a width) is now gone, not because the cost/benefit reasoning changed.

codexFinding4Declined.finding: Codex's cross-model review flagged that A12's chunk-detection uses `buf.indexOf('IDAT')`, which matches that literal byte sequence anywhere in the file -- including inside a metadata/text chunk (e.g. a tEXt chunk containing the literal string "IDAT") -- not only inside a real IDAT chunk header. A PNG carrying that string in metadata but with no genuine IDAT chunk would still register as having image data to A12.
codexFinding4Declined.declineRationale_teamLead: Declined by the team lead's own reasoning, recorded here: same threat model as above (honest hand-copy workflow, no adversary), and closing this specific finding requires walking the PNG chunk table properly (reading each chunk's length-prefixed header rather than substring-searching the whole buffer) -- a real but bounded scope increase, deliberately left out for a check whose design goal is fast and dependency-free.
codexFinding4Declined.declineRationale_qaIndependent: @qa reached the same DECLINE outcome via a sharper, independent argument recorded here because it changes the cost/benefit calculus, not just repeats the team lead's reasoning: a proper chunk-table walker would close THIS metadata-substring case, but it would NOT close the `declaredWidthForgery` gap immediately above -- that gap needs real zlib inflation and a decoded-content-vs-declared-dimension cross-check, which is a materially bigger lift than chunk-table walking alone. Since the narrow chunk-walking fix does not buy protection against the more realistic and more severe forgery gap, and both gaps sit outside the honest-hand-copy threat model in the first place, @qa's conclusion is that the narrow fix buys little relative to its cost -- reinforcing DECLINE rather than partially addressing it.
codexFinding4Declined.status: DECLINED, both independently and by team-lead/QA concurrence. Not fixed in this pass; not scheduled as a follow-up separate from `declaredWidthForgery` above, since the real remediation (a proper decoder) would address both gaps together, and neither is warranted under the stated threat model.

r23LockupComplianceSelfCheck.source: NOS Design, verbatim, issued against the NOS Site's EmblemBadge.tsx: it composes an SVG emblem with a text wordmark into a masthead lockup, which R14/4 forbids in terms -- "The artwork is never re-typeset and never re-tinted... Pick a colourway. Do not build a lockup." R20 adds that an emblem is a different artefact class from the lockup. Prescription: stop composing, start placing a supplied lockup file -- the wordmark is IN the artwork and is never typeset alongside it.
r23LockupComplianceSelfCheck.why this golden is checked, not just not: Team lead directive (2026-09-19): verify F8a's own compliance rather than assume it, because F8a places a supplied lockup file and 'on its face' complies -- but that must be confirmed against the actual golden spec and current implementation state, with file:line citations, not asserted.
r23LockupComplianceSelfCheck.implementationStateFound:
F8a is CONFIRMED still unimplemented in the live component, matching this golden's own `asset.note` ("@dev must NOT attempt to read or copy the branding/ file... treat public/images/nos-2027-logo-full-colour-vertical.png as a precondition dependency"). Read components/chrome/MegaMenu.tsx:132-149 directly (2026-09-19): the lead block still renders the PRE-F8a text pair -- a

{item.lead.eyebrow}

eyebrow (MegaMenu.tsx:136) and a separate serif {item.lead.leadLabel} heading (MegaMenu.tsx:137-143) -- with no /logo element present anywhere in that block. So this check evaluates this golden's PLANNED render spec (the `render` object above), not yet-written code -- there is nothing in the repo today that could violate or satisfy R14/4 for this feature.

planComplianceFindings.compositionCheck:
PASSES against R14/4 as specified. `render.wrapping` (above) states explicitly: the image sits INSIDE the existing IN PLACE OF the current eyebrow

+ serif heading pair -- i.e. a full swap-out, not an addition. `reading.ruling` (above) independently confirms this as FULL REPLACEMENT of both the eyebrow and the heading text with the single logo image, specifically because 'keeping the eyebrow text as a separate sibling above the image would duplicate what the artwork already says' -- the golden's author already reasoned through the R14/4-shaped failure mode (a text sibling next to the artwork) and ruled it out, independent of and prior to R23 being issued.
planComplianceFindings.altTextCheck: PASSES. `render.alt` ("National Orchid Show — Western Cape · 2027") and `render.altRationale` (above) confirm the alt string is transcribed from the artwork's own two text lines for accessibility purposes -- alt text describing artwork is correct practice, not composition, per WCAG (alt is non-visual, never rendered as a visible sibling). No risk here: R23's defect is a VISIBLE composed wordmark, and alt text is invisible by definition.
planComplianceFindings.leadMetaCheck: PASSES -- leadMeta (venue + date range) is a separate sibling BELOW the logo/lockup, not composed into it. `metaLineRuling` (above) is explicit that leadMeta is kept because the logo artwork itself does not carry the specific venue name or exact dates -- it is genuinely new information, not a re-statement of what the artwork already says, and it is not rendered inside the same visual unit as the artwork (no shared background/border/lockup treatment ties it to the image; it is plain text below, per the existing <span> markup at MegaMenu.tsx:144-148 which F8a's planned change does not alter). This is the one place a naive implementation COULD drift into an R14/4-shaped violation (e.g. if a future edit visually merged leadMeta into a bordered lockup box with the image) -- flagging as a watch-item for whoever implements F8a, not a present defect.
planComplianceFindings.theShowGroupCheck: PASSES, N/A to R23 -- `theShowGroupRuling` (above) keeps 'The Show' heading and its links list unchanged; it is a distinct navigational group below the lead block, not part of the logo/lockup treatment, and does not carry the show name or any text the artwork also carries.

r23LockupComplianceSelfCheck.verdict: NO DEFECT FOUND. F8a's golden spec, as written, complies with R14/4/R23: full replacement (not composition) of the eyebrow+heading text with the supplied lockup image, alt text used correctly (not as a composition substitute), and leadMeta kept separate and un-merged. Nothing in this golden needs to change to close R23 against our own feature. Because F8a remains unimplemented (blocked on the runtime asset per `asset.note`), there is no live code to fix even if a defect had been found -- this check is preventive, confirming the SPEC that will drive implementation doesn't inherit the same defect class NOS Design just found on the NOS Site.

domLoadVerificationRequirement.status: IMPLEMENTED as contract-f8.yaml A20, recorded 2026-09-21. NOT a suggestion, was never deferred to implementer discretion -- and it very nearly stayed unenforced: this requirement was written into the golden on 2026-09-19, explicitly binding on F8a's A1-A3 assertions once F8a was implemented, specifically BECAUSE the team lead foresaw it could be lost at the moment it came due. F8a was implemented after that (asset placed, MegaMenu.tsx rewritten, A1-A3 landed and went green) WITHOUT this requirement being enforced -- A1-A3 as actually written check element-presence-plus-src-attribute only, exactly the weak form this requirement exists to prevent (grepped directly: `naturalWidth` appears nowhere in e2e/mega-menu-f8-logo-and-tickets-rail.spec.ts as of 2026-09-21). It was caught by a team lead re-inspection after the fact, not by any gate -- the contract was fully green in the interim. RECORDED SO THE NEXT READER SEES THE PATTERN: this is the SECOND time this session a requirement written for a future implementation step was nearly lost at the moment that step actually landed (see A13-A19's F7-repair amendment above for the first -- a different mechanism, spec-locator breakage rather than a missed binding requirement, but the same underlying shape of 'a rule written ahead of the code it governs needs an explicit re-check when that code lands, not an assumption it was honoured'). Whoever next writes a golden requirement binding on work that hasn't started yet should consider whether the contract itself can enforce the binding (e.g. a assertion that fails, not vacuous-passes, until the dependent assertion exists) rather than relying on inspection to catch the gap a second time.
domLoadVerificationRequirement.gapThisCloses: @qa found a WRONG-DIRECTORY placement (e.g. the file landing at public/images/logo/nos-2027-logo-full-colour-vertical.png instead of asset.runtimeTargetPath above, public/images/nos-2027-logo-full-colour-vertical.png) is invisible to both existing gate-time checks: A10 reports the expected path missing but is informational-only (required: false, per its own expected-fail-until-placed design), and A12 vacuous-passes because nothing exists at the one path it is handed to check (per its own documented vacuous-pass-on-absence design, see assertionDecision.sequencing above). The contract gate goes fully green while the page 404s in production. This is a DIFFERENT failure shape from the caseSensitivityRuling fix above, and cannot be closed the same way: a file-level checker is only ever handed one path and can only ask 'does a valid file exist at exactly this path' -- it structurally cannot distinguish 'not placed anywhere' from 'placed correctly, but somewhere else', because it never searches, it only checks.
domLoadVerificationRequirement.requirement: When A1-A3 (the DOM assertions against the rendered mega-menu lead block) are written, they must verify the logo IMAGE ACTUALLY LOADED, not merely that an (or next/image-rendered) element exists in the DOM with the expected src attribute. The property to assert is the live element's naturalWidth > 0 -- and, where practical, that naturalWidth also matches the expected intrinsic width (3272px, per asset.note/source above, or a documented tolerance) -- read from the actual rendered element after load, not inferred from markup alone.
domLoadVerificationRequirement.whyMarkupAloneIsInsufficient: A 404'd or otherwise undecodable image still renders a syntactically correct element in the DOM with the correct src attribute and the correct layout box -- next/image reserves layout space from its width/height props (render.widthPx/heightPx above) regardless of whether any image bytes actually arrived over the network or decoded successfully. An assertion checking only for element-presence-plus-src-attribute would pass on a 404, a truncated download, or a corrupt file exactly as readily as on a correctly-loaded image -- this is the same 'assertion satisfiable without the property it claims to prove' defect class already named elsewhere in this golden (A9's framing, referenced in servingResolutionRuling.verifiedFacts and uncitedGap above) and in project memory feedback_contract_scoring_principles.
domLoadVerificationRequirement.whatThisSingleAssertionCloses: naturalWidth > 0, checked at the one point where it CAN be observed (a real browser having actually attempted to load and decode the file), closes several distinct failure modes at once, none of which gate-time file checks can reach: (1) wrong-directory placement, per `gapThisCloses` above; (2) a mis-cased filename on a case-sensitive host (Firebase App Hosting/Linux) that slipped past caseSensitivityRuling's local-machine check for any reason -- belt-and-suspenders against the same case class; (3) a truncated or otherwise corrupt file that happens to pass A12's structural IHDR-width read (A12 reads header bytes only, per acceptedLimitations.declaredWidthForgery above -- it never decodes); (4) the declaredWidthForgery class @qa demonstrated directly -- a forged IHDR width would decode successfully as some real (but different) image, so its real naturalWidth would disagree with the declared/expected width, which a naturalWidth-vs-expected comparison catches even though A12's raw header read cannot.
domLoadVerificationRequirement.relationshipToA12_notASubstitute: This assertion is the stated REASON A12 is allowed to stay cheap, header-only, and dependency-free (see acceptedLimitations above) rather than growing into a real decoder -- it is not redundant with A12, it is the other half of a two-point verification that A12 alone was never meant to complete. A12's job is to catch a bad asset BEFORE implementation, at gate time, when no DOM exists yet to inspect (F8a is unimplemented today -- there is nothing to load-check). The naturalWidth assertion's job is to catch what's left AFTER implementation, once a real browser can attempt a real load. Neither substitutes for the other: A12 alone leaves the gaps this section closes; the DOM assertion alone would leave a broken asset undetected for the entire period between it landing in public/images/ and any test run actually exercising the rendered page, with no informational pre-signal (A10's role) at all. Both are required.

knownUncoveredAtGateTimeToday.note: Recorded explicitly so a future reader does not mistake a currently-green gate as proof the runtime asset, once placed, is correctly located and loadable -- these are real, presently-open gaps, not hypotheticals, and they stay open until F8a is implemented and the naturalWidth assertion above is written and enforced.
knownUncoveredAtGateTimeToday.wrongDirectoryPlacement: Per `gapThisCloses` above -- a file placed at any path other than asset.runtimeTargetPath is invisible to both A10 and A12 today; the contract gate cannot currently detect it.
knownUncoveredAtGateTimeToday.trailingWhitespaceInFilename: A distinct, previously-unrecorded variant of the same 'checker is handed one exact path' limitation: a filename carrying trailing whitespace (e.g. a copy-paste artifact producing 'nos-2027-logo-full-colour-vertical.png ' with a trailing space, which macOS Finder and some browser downloads can silently introduce) fails an exact `test -f`/`existsSync` match against the expected path today -- so, unlike the case-sensitivity gap, this variant currently FAILS CLOSED (A10 correctly reports missing) rather than false-passing. Recorded here as a known-uncovered-at-gate-time case only in the sense that it is not specifically tested for and its exact failure behaviour (informational A10 miss vs. any future directory-listing-based check potentially matching it) has not been verified against a real fixture -- not because it is currently a silent false-pass like the other two.

leadMetaTestDefectRuling.status: RULED 2026-09-21, contract-f8.yaml A3 amended (fix specified, not yet implemented).
leadMetaTestDefectRuling.source: Codex GPT-5.5 cross-model review (mandatory per .claude/rules/workflow.md), finding 1 on e2e/mega-menu-f8-logo-and-tickets-rail.spec.ts's 'venue/date meta line still renders below the logo' test.
leadMetaTestDefectRuling.finding: Verified directly (Read tool, spec file lines 116-137): the test builds a `leadTrack` locator at line 126 and never uses it -- line 136 is a bare `void leadTrack;` to silence the unused-variable lint. What the test actually asserts (line 135) is only that the 'The Show' heading's bounding box sits below the logo's. It never locates leadMeta at all. Deleting leadMeta from MegaMenu.tsx entirely would leave this test green.
leadMetaTestDefectRuling.fix: data-testid="mega-menu-lead-meta" added to the leadMeta <span> (MegaMenu.tsx:156); test locates it directly and asserts visible + non-empty trimmed text + bounding-box position between the logo and the heading. Runs UNCONDITIONALLY, not guarded -- see distinctionFromFeatureRailMeta below for why this differs from the feature-rail meta line's legitimate conditional.
leadMetaTestDefectRuling.distinctionFromFeatureRailMeta: leadMeta = [venueName, dateRange].filter(Boolean).join(' · ') || null (MegaMenu.tsx:91-92) -- venueName alone is enough to make this non-null, and venueName is confirmed set in the current dataset (project memory project_national_show_venue: 'The Hangar, Stellenbosch Flying Club'). So leadMeta genuinely renders today, and an unconditional assertion is correct and safe. CORRECTED 2026-09-21: this note originally also described featureRailMeta (dateRange alone) as 'still-null' / 'genuinely null today' -- that was wrong, reached by reading a stale source comment (MegaMenu.tsx:84-88, dated 2026-09-10) rather than observing the live DOM. @dev's live instrumented run measured the real state: showDate/showEndDate ARE populated (metaCount: 1, text: '16–19 September 2027'). See f8-tickets-rail.json's metaLineTestDefectRuling.datasetStateCorrection for the full correction. The DISTINCTION drawn here still holds on its real grounds, independent of the retracted claim: leadMeta's unconditional assertion (A3) is justified because leadMeta has a venueName fallback that makes it non-null even if dates are absent, while A21's guard on featureRailMeta stays conditional because that value has no such fallback and COULD go null in the future (a CMS edit, a dataset reset) -- not because it is null now, which it is not.

repoWeightRuling.status: RULED 2026-09-21, no action taken -- the public/images/ copy is accepted as-is. CORRECTED 2026-09-21 (same day) after the team lead supplied a measured fact this ruling's original reasoning did not have: kept below as `originalReasoningSupersededInPart`, replaced by `correctedFinding` as the operative basis.
repoWeightRuling.question: Whether copying a ~5MB PNG into public/images/ (a directory whose largest previously-tracked file was orchid-purple.jpg at ~3.1MB) is a repo-weight problem worth addressing before this feature closes.

correctedFinding.source: Team lead, 2026-09-21, measured directly: `git hash-object` on both `branding/National Show 2027/Logo/NOS-2027-logo-full-colour-vertical.png` and `public/images/nos-2027-logo-full-colour-vertical.png` returns the SAME blob SHA (1d9a0a43ef2af49ef4c19c9eae3de79193388ee0), and `git cat-file -e` confirms that blob is already in the object database via the branding/ path's existing tracking.
correctedFinding.meaning: Git addresses content by hash, not by path -- two tracked paths with byte-identical content share ONE blob in the object database. Committing the public/images/ copy therefore adds a new TREE ENTRY (a path -> blob pointer, bytes on the order of the path string) but NOT a new BLOB -- the ~5MB of actual content is already paid for by the branding/ path's own existing tracking. This supersedes `originalReasoningSupersededInPart` below, which reasoned from file-size comparison (duplication is real but small relative to an already-large repo) rather than from the actual git storage mechanism (there is close to no duplication at the object-database level at all).
correctedFinding.inversionWorthRecording: Downscaling/re-exporting the asset to 'save weight' would make the repo BIGGER, not smaller -- a derived file has different bytes, hence a NEW blob, added on top of the original blob (which stays tracked at its branding/ path regardless, and stays in git history regardless of whether anything currently references it). The cheapest option by repo weight and R22's serving-resolution requirement (place a genuine derivative of the master, never a re-export) are the SAME action -- placing the unmodified master. These two considerations do not trade off against each other here; recording this so a future editor doesn't 'optimise' the asset on a reasonable-sounding but wrong intuition about file size.

originalReasoningSupersededInPart.status: Superseded by correctedFinding above for the BLOB-dedup point specifically. Kept for provenance -- its file-size framing was not wrong, just less precise than the direct blob-hash measurement; its next/image serving-behaviour reasoning (below) is UNCHANGED and still stands, not superseded.
originalReasoningSupersededInPart.factsConsulted: From .agent/memory/scratch/research-menu-system-layout4-f8-asset-provenance.md, finding 4: the source file is ALREADY git-tracked at its branding/ path today (branding/National Show 2027/Logo/NOS-2027-logo-full-colour-vertical.png, 4,990,718 bytes, ranking 12th/13th-largest tracked file in the repo already), and the whole repo is already 8.6GB working-tree / 430MB packed, with at least 11 other tracked files larger than this one (branding/ zips and PDFs, design/ zips, evidence screenshots).

repoWeightRuling.servingBehaviourConsulted: next/image with a fixed width={200} height={176} and no `sizes` prop places this in the 'fixed-size image' branch (Next.js docs, cited in the research file): it generates a 1x/2x srcset and serves an optimizer-resized, re-encoded (AVIF/WebP-negotiated) derivative through /_next/image, not the raw 5MB file, to any real browser request. The 5MB weight is a repo/deploy-bundle storage cost, not a runtime bandwidth cost to site visitors. This point is unaffected by the blob-dedup correction above -- it is about serving, not storage.

deployBundleCostRuling.question: Firebase App Hosting ships everything under public/ into the deploy bundle regardless of git blob-dedup (a working checkout materializes the full 5MB file on disk at build/deploy time, whatever git's internal storage looks like) -- does that 5MB matter for this project's deploy?
deployBundleCostRuling.reasoning: public/images/ already carries several multi-MB files at comparable order of magnitude (5 orchid JPGs plus 6 SAOC logo PNGs per the research inventory; orchid-purple.jpg alone is 3.13MB) -- this file becomes the largest in that directory, but not by a new order of magnitude, and the directory as a whole is already a multi-file, multi-MB asset set by design (marketing photography + brand logos), not a lean/minimal one this file would be uniquely anomalous in. Firebase App Hosting serves static /public assets via its CDN layer, not through the SSR function's own cold-start path -- a large static asset does not weigh on server response latency the way a large SERVER-SIDE dependency would. No documented deploy-size ceiling for this project's Firebase App Hosting tier has been hit or is close to being hit (no evidence consulted or cited establishing a limit is near); this is a single ~5MB addition to a public/images/ directory whose existing files already sum to double-digit MB.
deployBundleCostRuling.ruling: Accepted as-is, not a deploy concern for this feature. If public/ as a whole grows materially further (more brand assets, more show-year logos in future editions), that becomes a real question about asset-directory hygiene (e.g. moving to a CDN/object-storage-backed image source rather than bundling raster brand assets in-repo) -- but that is a structural decision for the project as it scales, not something this single ~5MB, already-necessary asset triggers on its own. Recorded as a watch-item, not actioned.

repoWeightRuling.ruling: No action required for this feature. (1) Git object-database weight: the public/images/ copy shares its blob with the already-tracked branding/ original (correctedFinding above) -- committing it adds a tree entry, not a new ~5MB blob. (2) Deploy-bundle weight: accepted, not anomalous for this project's public/images/ directory or its Firebase App Hosting serving model (deployBundleCostRuling above). (3) next/image does not serve the raw bytes to visitors regardless of either of the above. (4) public/images/ is exactly where a runtime-servable asset belongs per this project's own Next.js convention (Next only serves /public) -- there is no alternate correct location. Deferring, not declining: whether branding/ as a whole (258MB, git-tracked, containing a 56MB zip and two 40+MB emblem PNGs) should be pruned from git history or moved to LFS/external storage is a real, separate question this ruling does NOT resolve -- it is a repo-hygiene decision affecting Brad's whole active design workstream (project memory project_design_folders_brad_active), not a call for this feature's contract to make unilaterally. Recorded as a backlog candidate, not actioned here.
